headline_marked: [[Chittagong waterlogging project extends to 11 years]] due to hasty planning, cost revised to BDT 8.59B
headline: Chittagong waterlogging project extends to 11 years due to hasty planning, cost revised to BDT 8.59B
summary: Originally a three-year project, the Chittagong Development Authority's (CDA) waterlogging alleviation initiative will now take 11 years to complete, with its cost rising from BDT 5.61 billion to BDT 8.59 billion.
details: A critical waterlogging alleviation project in Chittagong, initially planned for three years, is now projected to take 11 years to complete. The project's cost has significantly increased from an initial BDT 5.61 billion to BDT 8.59 billion.

Named 'Canal Re-excavation, Expansion, Renovation, and Development for Waterlogging Alleviation in Chittagong City', the Chittagong Development Authority (CDA) has set a new deadline of June 2028. This revised plan has been sent to the Ministry of Housing and Public Works for final approval.
The project's original cost was BDT 5.61 billion when approved in August 2017. It was first revised to BDT 8.62 billion in December 2023, and now stands at BDT 8.59 billion in the second revision.

Despite four ongoing waterlogging projects over the past 8-10 years, costing over BDT 10.40 billion by March, Chittagong continues to face severe flooding. The city experienced its most severe waterlogging this year on April 28.

Experts attribute the problems to flaws in the initial planning phase, stating that comprehensive field surveys, water flow analysis, tidal considerations, and integrated assessments of canals, drains, and reservoirs were not adequately conducted.
Due to the lack of detailed surveys and studies, physical work on the project could not commence for the first 1.5 to 2 years. Subsequent field work continued to reveal new problems and complexities.
As of May, the CDA's waterlogging project has achieved 98% progress. However, work on two of the 36 canals, Hijra and Jamal Khan canals, remains unfinished.

Ahmad Moinuddin, CDA's Executive Engineer and Project Director, explained that the latest revision was necessary due to financing complexities. The initial plan included CDA's own funds and government loans.

Under the new proposal, nearly the entire BDT 8.59 billion will come as government grants, with BDT 103 million as a 5% interest loan repayable over 20 years. The government will disburse the grants in phases over two years, necessitating the project extension.

To manage costs, work on several sectors like silt traps, footpaths, and bitumen roads has been reduced, saving approximately BDT 488 million. However, expenses in 13 other sectors, including canal excavation, drainage infrastructure, and bridge construction, have increased by BDT 453 million.

Engineer Delwar Majumder, former chairman of the Engineers Institution Bangladesh (IEB) Chittagong Centre, criticized CDA for taking on the project hastily without proper surveys. He noted this led to initial delays and ongoing issues, making time extension unavoidable.

headline_marked: [[River swallowed school]], 73 students now learn on flood embankment in Bogura
headline: River swallowed school, 73 students now learn on flood embankment in Bogura
summary: The century-old Chakratinath Government Primary School in Bogura's Sonatala Upazila was lost to river erosion, forcing 73 students to continue their education in a makeshift tin shed on a flood control embankment.
details: River erosion by the Jamuna is relentlessly destroying homes, arable land, and now educational institutions in Bangladesh. The century-old Chakratinath Government Primary School in Bogura's Sonatala Upazila has been completely swallowed by the river.

Following the school's disappearance, 73 students are now receiving their lessons in a temporary tin shed built on a flood control embankment. This highlights the community's resilience and determination to continue education despite immense challenges.

The adjacent Purba Sujaitpur Government Primary School-cum-flood shelter is also under imminent threat from ongoing river erosion. This situation underscores the continuous struggle for education, livelihoods, and survival for people in Bangladesh's riverine areas.
